brief_context: The specific site in the City used for Mansion House.
brief_extract:
History of the site
Formerly the Lord Mayor lived in his private house in the City, but after the Great Fire John Evelyn made proposals to Charles II for a residence for the Lord Mayor and the site chosen some 70 years later was almost the same. In 1735 George Dance, Clerk of the City's Works, prepared plans for the Mansion House on the Stock Market site which derived its name from a pair of stocks for malefactors and was built in Henry II's reign for the sale of fish and flesh. On November 9, 1752, the Lord Mayor, Alderman Crisp Gascoyne, was first lodged in the Mansion House following a ball at Guildhall after the Lord Mayor's Banquet, but few of the original fittings and furnishings have survived.

brief_extract:
The Egyptian Hall
The Egyptian Hall
The principal room is the Egyptian Hall which was based on Palladio's interpretation of a great architectural treatise by Vitruvius, Julius Caesar's military engineer in the African war who thought that a hall with pillars and clerestory was of Egyptian origin. The name Egyptian Hall was given by Lord Burlington to his Great Room of the Assembly Rooms at York in 1736 and this inspired George Dance. The Great Hall in the Mansion House has sixteen massive Corinthian columns with a great cornice on which rests a coved ceiling in blue and ivory.

brief_context: Mentioned as a source of cheap gas for heating.
brief_extract: Between 1966 and 1970 there was tremendous growth in electric central heating. Gas developed rapidly because of cheap North Sea Gas which is substantially denied to the power stations. From 1963 to 1971 storage radiators were important and today their night load is equivalent to almost a quarter of the daytime total maximum demand.

brief_context: Location where electrical development research is undertaken.
brief_extract:
Utilisation research
At present the more electricity we sell the more money we lose but with an eye to the future we must consider the total field of legitimate electrical development and we must maintain our interest in markets and continue to promote. Research is undertaken at Capenhurst and some of the results have been Centralec, a system which uses a solid core and is similar to Electricaire but has an air to water heat exchanger; a thermal storage wall which in essence is a storage radiator occupying a whole wall and will be on the market in 2 or 3 years; and vacuum radiators using the principle of a vacuum as the best possible form of insulation and giving out variable heat according to the controlled degree of vacuum maintained. Importance of thermal insulation
Thermal insulation is important for the economic use of all forms of energy, and typically collaboration between the Midlands Electricity Board and a developer is producing homes in which the heat losses are reduced to less than one-third, that is from around 14 kW to 4 kW.

brief_extract:
The first sulphur battery test vehicle, in operation prior to its showing on BBC television 'Tomorrow's World' programme, greatly impressed everyone. VISIT TO LONGANNET POWER STATION, KINCARDINE
by MRS MARY SMITH, Magazine Reporter, Edinburgh Afternoon Branch

This power station, on the North bank of the River Forth, is the newest and largest of the SSEB's coal-fired power stations and occupies 220 acres, the land having been reclaimed from the river with boiler ash from the nearby Kincardine Power Station. This is an ideal site in that (a) of the 5,000,000 tons of coal burned yearly over half comes from the NCB Longannet Mine Complex and is delivered direct to the surface through an inclined shaft, and the remainder is brought from nearby mines by means of trains with special bottom-opening wagons which unload automatically while moving slowly through the unloading bay, a former Ordnance Depot providing a level area for coal storage; (b) the 327 million litres of cooling water travelling through the condensers every hour are taken from the river having passed through screens which extract unwanted matter and protect salmon smolt, and the cooling water is discharged from the power station into a wide part of the river where the heat it has acquired causes no damage; (c) the 4,350 tons of residual ash per day are mixed with river water and pumped to disposal lagoons for land reclamation.

brief_context: Refers to the safety of electric appliances in the UK.
article_title: Address by Sir Geoffrey Howe, QC, MP
brief_extract: The Department of Trade and Industry had commissioned a study on Domestic Meter Reading and the report concluded that automatic remote reading systems would not be competitive for many years. The great majority of domestic electric appliances in this country are safe when sold but this is not universally true and there is no general statutory requirement that goods offered for sale must be electrically safe, although there are regulations on guards for electric fires, the colour coding of flexes and the safety of electric blankets. While it has been Home Office policy to rely on voluntary action by the trade to ensure safety, many people, particularly in consumer organisations, think that there should be a general statutory requirement to cover all electrical goods coming on the market.

brief_context: Refers to member-states of the European Economic Community (EEC).
article_title: Address by Sir Geoffrey Howe, QC, MP
brief_extract: The accident figures are not high in relation to the number of electrical products in use every day, but we need to consider whether reliance on largely voluntary action can continue to be regarded as sufficient. An EEC directive will be implemented by August 1974 to remove those technical barriers to trade which are created by different laws and practices relating to safety in different member-states of the Community. Member governments are under an obligation to take what steps they consider necessary to ensure that electrical equipment may be sold only if it is safe, but individual governments may decide how best to meet their obligations.

All who have had difficulty in opening, say, a packet of biscuits or are critical of the way in which modern foodstuffs are packed and presented will be interested in a recent conference at Queen Elizabeth College arranged by the Good Housekeeping Institute and the Housewives’ Trust. brief_context: Historical origins of baking eggs date back to Grecian times.
brief_extract:
Baking Eggs
The tenth of a dozen egg information sheets
Baking eggs, one of the oldest methods of cooking, dates back to Grecian times when heated salt was used to set beaten eggs in a pastry case. Through the Middle Ages, eggs were baked in "coffynes" (pastry cases without lids) and, although the eggs used were beaten, the basic cookery method was the forerunner of a dish which is appealing, yet perhaps not as often prepared as one would expect.

brief_context: Cocotte is the French name of the dish.
brief_extract: Through the Middle Ages, eggs were baked in "coffynes" (pastry cases without lids) and, although the eggs used were beaten, the basic cookery method was the forerunner of a dish which is appealing, yet perhaps not as often prepared as one would expect. A Better Place to Live

WE have all long been concerned with making homes better places in which to live from the point of view of labour-saving, comfort, safety and aesthetic appearance inside and out, and now we are beginning to look further afield and to realise that good living conditions for our society depend not only on the location, design and equipment of homes but on the treatment of the natural resources of this country, the flora and fauna, and the landscape in general. While we have for the most part eliminated the grime and gloom resulting from the earlier Industrial Revolution in Britain's towns and cities and have eradicated the slums which grew up in its train, the rapid developments of modern technology have presented us with a new set of problems making their impact on the environment. We are also realising that damage to the environment now takes place at an unprecedented rate and the effects are often irreversible.

Electricity and the Environment

by MARY GEORGE, MBE, Companion IEE, Director EAW

Church by Dean Bridge, Edinburgh, now a sub-station of the South of Scotland Electricity Board

THE three largest publicly owned electricity authorities in the English speaking world (the Ontario Hydro Authority in Canada, the Tennessee Valley Authority in the USA, and our own Central Electricity Generating Board) met together recently to discuss ways and means of aligning their obligation to provide electricity in the quantity demanded at the lowest possible price with the need to interfere as little as possible with the environment. Not surprisingly the conference did not come up with any definite answer to the question: what is the right price to pay for environmental protection?

article_title: THE MAT WITHOUT A WELCOME: Electricity protects your home
brief_extract:
THE MAT WITHOUT A WELCOME

Electricity protects your home

by WINIFRED E. PORTER, Member of EAW National Executive Committee and President of Yorkshire Area Federation

Photographs by courtesy of Leeds City Police

Chubb Alarm pressure mat fits under carpet

HAVING equipped ourselves with many expensive electrical appliances and owning many other valuable possessions, do we provide ourselves with the means of safeguarding them? We read of theft and vandalism, yet many of us still move in that cloud-cuckoo-land of 'It will never happen to me.' But those members of the EAW to whom it has happened, and there are, alas, far too many of them, know the traumatic effect of returning to their much-loved home to find it denuded of treasured possessions and ravished by vandals.

brief_context: Location where a six-week electrical course was conducted.
brief_extract:
STUDENT
NEWS

Electrical course at Bedford School

A special six-week course on home electricity was conducted by Mrs Joyce Mackenzie, Assistant EAW Organiser, Eastern Area, at Lyncroft School, Bedford. It was for boys and girls of 12 years old and covered planning a small flat and choosing the electrical appliances; electricity from the power station to the home; home circuits; volts, amps and watts; colour coding, flexibles, fuses, plugs and thermostats; appliance loading; the meter and the cost of electricity, and the principles of cookers and refrigerators.

THE Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust has awarded a major university scholarship and two minor scholarships each tenable for three years from October 1973. brief_context: Location of Merchant Taylors' School for Girls.
brief_extract: Her present intention is to qualify as a metallurgist. A pupil of Merchant Taylors’ School for Girls, Crosby, she is an all-rounder as well as distinguishing herself academically by gaining one of the school’s coveted Harrison (Foundation) Scholarships. Her interests cover several sports, choral singing and debating and she has a strong social sense, having taken part in an Old Folks’ Concert and assisting two elderly ladies regularly with their weekly shopping.

brief_context: Hometown of scholarship winner Helen Louise Donald.
brief_extract: Her interests cover several sports, choral singing and debating and she has a strong social sense, having taken part in an Old Folks’ Concert and assisting two elderly ladies regularly with their weekly shopping. brief_extract:
M. BURNS, Honorary Secretary, Birmingham Branch

location_standardised: Coventry, West Midlands, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: City supplied with electricity from Hams Hall.
article_title: VISIT TO HAMS HALL 'C' POWER STATION
brief_extract: When producing its full and continuous supply of electricity to the grid system 'C' Station consumes approximately 5,000 tons of coal or approximately 105 million cubic feet of natural gas per day. Electricity generated at Hams Hall 'C' Station is supplied to the cities of Birmingham and Coventry, and by the grid system to any national load centre. This visit made members realise what a tremendous amount of power there is behind that 'flick of a switch'.

brief_extract:
VISIT TO HIGH PEAK COLLEGE OF FURTHER EDUCATION AND CATERING, BUXTON
by MRS T. HASLAM, Magazine Secretary, Mansfield Branch

At this college which caters for both boys and girls, members were welcomed, by one of the lecturers before being divided into two parties, each in charge of two students and the tour started with the students' kitchen which contained mainly electric ovens and grills, refrigerators and other ancillary equipment. Next came the kitchen where students were preparing lunches not only for themselves but also for the staff and visitors; then the typing room where half the typewriters were electrically operated; the shorthand classroom; hairdressing room, and the commerce room where students receive incoming queries in Russian, French, Italian, Spanish, German, etc, to which they have to reply in the corresponding language.

brief_context: Source of banana cargoes coming into Empress Dock.
brief_extract: This is acknowledged to be one of the finest passenger reception stations in the world and is nearly quarter-mile long. Empress Dock was opened by Queen Victoria in 1890 and is used by Fyffes Line, with cargoes of bananas from the West Indies. The Inner Dock was reclaimed in 1966.

brief_context: Destination for roll on/off services from Alexandra Dock.
brief_extract: The Inner Dock was reclaimed in 1966. The Princess Alexandra Dock was opened in 1967 and is a base for the roll on/off services to Le Havre, Cherbourg, and the ports of Bilbao, Lisbon and Casablanca. The King George V Dry Dock was opened by King George V on July 26, 1933, and, measuring 1,200 ft long, 135 ft wide and 59 ft deep, it is one of the largest dry docks in the world and can accommodate liners of 100,000 tons.

brief_context: Capital of Trinidad where Mary George arrived by plane.
brief_extract: Immediately she suggested that I should pay another visit to Trinidad when I was on the other side of the Atlantic, and in due course I received a very warm invitation from our sister association which I could not resist as I still had very happy memories of my previous visit eight years ago. I found the same friendly welcome awaiting me and the same spicy smell in the air when I flew into Port-of-Spain, the capital of Trinidad, for my second visit, and I was again taken off by Leslie Dookhie, the General Manager of the Trinidad and Tobago Electricity Commission (always known as T and TEC), and his dear wife, Denise, to stay in their charming hillside home with its garden where the roses bloom all the year round. There to greet me from the EAW was a magnificent arrangement of poinsettias, lilies, orchids and other tropical flowers which only a middle eastern oil sheikh could afford to buy in London.

brief_context: Location of a newly formed EAW branch visited.
brief_extract: I was also presented with a fairly formidable programme but I did not mind this because I wanted in any case to meet as many of the members and branches as possible during my brief four days. One 'must' was to visit the very recently formed branch at Arima and to install the officers. With this new branch the Association now has four branches in Trinidad and the one in Tobago.

There were addresses of welcome from the parish priest, the local member of parliament, the representative of the local Council and myself, and then the very charming and efficient Branch Chairman, Daphne Gilkes-Sotilleo, introduced the other officers and there were many greetings and gifts exchanged. By the end I was surrounded with presents as though it were Christmas especially as the near-by Tunapuna Branch had joined in the party and the presentations. brief_context: Main island location for the first part of the report.
brief_extract: Branch in the south of the island and as we drove across the country I realised that Trinidad also has its traffic problems which have increased in recent years just like ours. We crawled bonnet to bumper in slow procession along the palm edged roads with storm clouds lowering over the hills and occasional bursts of rain.

brief_context: Building where the author met the local Mayor.
brief_extract: Fortunately, our car was air conditioned because the humid heat and petrol fumes would have been unbearable. We arrived at the Town Hall of San Fernando rather belatedly but in time to pay a courtesy call on the Mayor and drink a glass of fruit juice with him in his Parlour. Then we went on to the branch meeting where again there were speeches and presentations.

brief_context: Town where the branch meeting and dinner were held.

brief_context: Origin country of one of the local school teachers.
brief_extract: Among the guests were two charming Roman Catholic nuns who taught in local schools. One of them who came from Ireland turned out to be an expert on horror films and fast cars. She also claimed to have some electrical knowledge and to be called in when the lights failed in her school.

location_standardised: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago
brief_context: Venue for dinner and a social coffee party.
brief_extract: I hope the Branch Chairman took note of her as a potential member. Among the other social functions arranged for me was a dinner at the Hilton Hotel where we sat beside the bathing pool under the starlit sky, listened to one of the most famous steel bands on the island and watched the limbo dancing. The only trouble with steel bands is that they completely inhibit conversation.

brief_context: The author's next destination and subject of second section.
brief_extract:
When I left Trinidad having been showered with gifts and almost drowned in rum punch during my four days, it was very much a question of 'au revoir' from our fellow members there because they are most excited by the thought of our Golden Jubilee and are already thinking of chartering a plane to come over and join our celebrations. Barbados
My next port of call was Barbados which I had not visited before and where I thought I might try to sow some EAW seeds. John Nelson, Managing Director of the Barbados Light and Power Company, whose parent company is Canadian, was extremely kind and hospitable and I spent a pleasant evening in the company of him and his wife.

brief_context: Home of the parent company of Barbados Light and Power.
Island mentioned as a beautiful holiday destination.
brief_extract: We shall see. It would certainly be nice if a Barbadian EAW were formed because they would be near-by neighbours for the Trinidad and Tobago Association. Barbados is a perfect place for a holiday.

brief_context: Discussing the transition to the metric system in the UK.
brief_extract: The Board are aiming to help these play their part in making the change to metric as smooth as possible for everybody. The reasons for Britain going metric are simple. Years ago, when most of our business was done with people who used the same imperial measurement system as we did, change did not make sense.

brief_context: Mentioned as a trade partner for Britain.
brief_extract: A growing volume of our overseas business is with metric countries. In 1958 about a third of Britain's trade was with western Europe. By 1971 this had increased to nearly half.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding its Metric Conversion Bill before Congress.
brief_extract: Nearly all world trade is now between countries which have chosen metric. In America there is a Metric Conversion Bill before Congress now. Hand in hand with these world developments has been an increasing demand for goods to be made to international standards.

location_standardised: London, Greater London, England, United Kingdom
brief_context: Address for Her Majesty's Stationery Office.
brief_extract: The Metrication Board recently published its fourth report entitled Going Metric: Progress in 1972. (Available from Her Majesty's Stationery Office, 49 High Holborn, WC1V 6HB and branches. Also through booksellers.) The report concludes that the housewife would gain from an orderly and speedy changeover and that it is in the country's interest to press forward vigorously with the metric change.

brief_context: Site of a nature trail mentioned in the image caption.
brief_extract:
Power and the Environment

Nature trail at Drakelow Power Station, near Burton-on-Trent

IT would be nonsense to suppose that an industrial undertaking which in 90 years has grown from nothing to one which invests more than £1 million daily could be run without some impact on the environment but by good management that impact is small indeed compared with electricity’s economic and social benefit. The industry is not hungry for land; the area required for new power station and substation sites is only a trifling percentage of the land developed for all other purposes and sites acquired in the earlier day of the industry are used and re-used for different operational purposes as the original plant upon them is superseded.
